subtype: Approach: saying sorry for his part and asking to play again [Action]
passage: Vasudev reached school ten minutes early and waited by the gate for his friend Pervez. His stomach felt tight. When Pervez walked in, Vasudev stepped forward. "I'm sorry I laughed at your tiffin. I didn't mean it to hurt you." Pervez said nothing for a moment and looked at his shoes. Vasudev took a breath and went on. "Can we play football at recess, you and me on one team?" Pervez shrugged, but the corner of his mouth moved. "Only if I get goalkeeper." "Done," said Vasudev. They walked to class together, not talking much, but not angry any more either.

qa.q: Where did Vasudev wait for Pervez?
qa.a: Vasudev waited by the gate.

qa.q: What was Vasudev feeling when he stepped forward to speak to Pervez?
qa.a: Vasudev was nervous, shown by the tight stomach and the deep breath he took before speaking. 😰

qa.q: What other approach could Vasudev use if Pervez stayed silent, and why?
qa.a: Vasudev could give Pervez a little time and try again at lunch, or write a short note. Space can help a hurt friend feel ready to answer.

qa.q: How does Pervez seem to feel about the apology?
qa.a: Pervez was quiet at first and looked at his shoes, so it may have been hard to trust it, but the small smile and the goalkeeper request suggest Pervez was softening.

grounding: A boy apologises for his part in the quarrel the next day and asks his friend to play football at recess.

subtype: Approach: waiting for the other friend to say sorry first [Pitfall]
passage: In the schoolyard in Addis Ababa, Dalia stood with her arms crossed. She was sure the argument with her friend Abebe about the skipping rope was Abebe's fault. "If Abebe wants to talk, Abebe knows where I am," she told herself. Across the yard, Abebe was thinking the very same words. On Monday they did not speak. On Tuesday they sat at opposite ends of the bench. By Thursday, the other girls were choosing sides and whispering, and lunch felt very long. Dalia ate slowly, watching the rope swing without her. She missed the laughing. But her pride was louder, so she kept quiet.

qa.q: What was the argument between Dalia and Abebe about?
qa.a: The argument was about the skipping rope.

qa.q: What is Dalia feeling by Thursday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Dalia feels lonely and misses the laughing; eating slowly and watching the rope swing without her show it, although pride keeps Dalia quiet. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dalia try, and why might it work?
qa.a: Dalia could speak first and say what she felt, because someone has to break the silence. Asking a teacher to help them talk could also work.

qa.q: How do the other girls affect the situation?
qa.a: The other girls are choosing sides and whispering, which makes the split feel bigger and more public for both Dalia and Abebe.

grounding: Each friend waits for the other to say sorry first, so days pass in loneliness while the other girls pick sides.

subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Suraj slammed his bag down. "My friend Elizabeth was so unfair about the cricket score," he told the whole class at lunch. "Ask anyone." Two boys nodded.

Wednesday. Suraj heard a new version in the corridor: Elizabeth had cheated and refused to admit it. He had never said that. He felt strangely uneasy, but he kept quiet.

Friday. Elizabeth stood at the classroom door with red eyes. "Why are you telling everyone I cheat?" Suraj tried to explain, but the story had already grown past him, and Elizabeth walked away without waiting.

qa.q: What did Suraj say Elizabeth was unfair about?
qa.a: Suraj said Elizabeth was unfair about the cricket score.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel when he heard the new version in the corridor?
qa.a: Suraj felt uneasy, because the story had grown into something he never said and he no longer controlled it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Suraj have used, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could have spoken to Elizabeth directly about the cricket score, since talking to the person involved stops the story from spreading. He could also ask a teacher to help settle the score.

qa.q: How does the spreading story feel to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Elizabeth is hurt and angry, shown by the red eyes at the door and the question about cheating, because Elizabeth's name is now attached to something untrue.

grounding: A boy tells the class his side of the fight, the story spreads and grows, and the friend becomes angrier so the fight is harder to mend.

subtype: Approach: writing a small note if talking feels too hard [Action]
passage: Class teacher's note, Thursday. During free reading I saw Pema, the quietest girl in the row, take out a torn page and write something slowly, crossing out two lines. After two days of not speaking to her friend Vikas, Pema had shouted at recess on Tuesday and seemed too embarrassed to say anything. Pema folded the page small and slipped it into Vikas's desk, then went back to a book without turning a page. Vikas found it after the bell and read it twice: "I'm sorry I yelled. Want to be friends again?" By afternoon Vikas had left a reply on Pema's desk. I did not step in. Both seem lighter.

qa.q: Where did Pema put the folded page?
qa.a: Pema slipped it into Vikas's desk.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling while writing and slipping the note away?
qa.a: Pema was probably shy and embarrassed, shown by writing slowly, crossing out lines and pretending to read afterwards.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pema use if a note does not get an answer, and why?
qa.a: Pema could ask the teacher to help the two of them talk, or wait for a calm moment to speak in person. A helper can make a hard conversation easier.

qa.q: How does Vikas experience the note?
qa.a: Vikas read it twice and left a reply, so the note gave Vikas time to take in the apology and answer without pressure.

grounding: A shy girl who finds speaking hard writes a short note asking to be friends, and the note gives the friend time to feel and reply.

subtype: Approach: asking a teacher for help to talk it out [Revision]
passage: Note from the class teacher. Gargi came to me at the end of Monday, hands twisted together. She had tried to make up with Raghav at the water tank, but within a minute both were shouting again. "We can't fix it alone," she said. "Will you help?" I asked them to come in after school. I sat between them and set one rule: each of us speaks while the others listen. Raghav went first, fast and angry. Then Gargi told her side. By the end Raghav was staring at the floor, and Gargi's shoulders had dropped. They left together, still awkward, but talking.

qa.q: Where did Gargi and Raghav's first attempt end in shouting?
qa.a: Their first attempt ended in shouting at the water tank.

qa.q: What did Gargi realise after the shouting, and how might Gargi have felt?
qa.a: Gargi realised they could not fix it alone; twisted hands suggest Gargi felt worried and a little ashamed of the shouting.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Gargi try if the talk with the teacher still stays tense, and why?
qa.a: Gargi could write down what matters most to say, or wait a few days before trying again with calmer feelings. Both could work because they slow the anger.

qa.q: How might Raghav see the talk with the teacher?
qa.a: Raghav went first and fast, then stared at the floor while Gargi spoke, so Raghav may have felt defensive and then thoughtful once listening.

grounding: Her first attempt to make up ends in shouting, so she notices they cannot fix it alone and asks the class teacher to help them take turns speaking.

subtype: Approach: offering a fair fix like taking turns [Action]
passage: At the edge of the wheat fields behind the village school, Hemant and Tushar stood nose to nose. "I'm captain!" "No, I am!" The other boys sat on the grass, waiting with the ball. Hemant was about to storm off when Tushar said, "If I'm captain today, you're captain tomorrow. Then we swap." Hemant thought. It sounded fair. "Me first tomorrow?" "Fine," said Tushar. They shook hands, picked teams, and the game began. On the next day Hemant chose the sides, and Tushar lined up behind him without a word. The fight did not come back that week.

qa.q: How did Hemant and Tushar decide who is captain?
qa.a: Whoever is captain today, the other is captain tomorrow, and then they swap.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling just before Tushar suggested a swap?
qa.a: Hemant was angry and about to storm off, showing how much being captain mattered.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the boys use, and why?
qa.a: They could toss a coin or ask the other boys to vote, since both give a fair answer quickly. Sharing the job with two captains is another option.

qa.q: How do the boys waiting on the grass see the argument?
qa.a: The other boys sit and wait with the ball, so they probably feel bored and impatient, and want the fight settled so the game can start.

grounding: The fight is about who is captain, and the boys agree to alternate the job each day so both are treated fairly.

subtype: Approach: pretending nothing happened and acting normal [Thinking]
passage: Ganga, come and sit. Your grandfather Francis once had a fight with his friend Anthony over a lost marble. I was ten. The next morning I said to myself: if I act as if nothing happened, maybe it will all melt away. So I walked up to Anthony at the gate and held out half a banana chip packet. "Want some?" Anthony took a chip and we chewed together. It worked, that day. But Anthony's eyes stayed on the ground, and he did not laugh at my jokes. Weeks later I learned he had been waiting for me to say something about the marble.

qa.q: What did Francis offer Anthony at the gate?
qa.a: Francis offered half a packet of banana chips.

qa.q: What did Francis want to happen when the chips were held out at the gate?
qa.a: Francis hoped that acting as if nothing had happened would make the fight melt away, which shows a wish to avoid an awkward talk.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could Francis have made differently, and why might it help?
qa.a: Francis could have mentioned the marble and said sorry along with sharing the chips, because saying it aloud would have shown that Anthony's hurt mattered.

qa.q: How did the sharing of chips feel to Anthony?
qa.a: It felt like a kind gesture but not enough; Anthony had been waiting for Francis to say something about the marble.

grounding: A child invites a friend to share a snack as if there was no fight, which works for a day but leaves the hurt unspoken.

subtype: Approach: copying rules from a game they already know [Thinking]
passage: The terrace had a clothesline down the middle and only half an hour of light left. Sonali clapped for attention. "We don't have time to invent everything. Let's take from games we know." Parveen counted on her fingers. "Kabaddi has a home line and a chant. Tag has someone who is 'it'." "So a raider runs across and tries to touch someone," said Sonali, "and everyone else tries to tag the raider before they get back." The little ones were nodding. Within ten minutes, they were playing a game with kabaddi's line and tag's chasing, and nobody argued about what a rule meant.

qa.q: What did Parveen say kabaddi has?
qa.a: Parveen said kabaddi has a home line and a chant.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about the time left, and why did she want to borrow from known games?
qa.a: Sonali felt pressured by the little light and time left, so she wanted to start quickly by borrowing rules instead of inventing everything.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use to add to the game, and why?
qa.a: They could play a short trial round and change any rule that is confusing, because playing shows problems faster than talking. They could also let the youngest suggest a rule.

qa.q: How might the younger children see this plan?
qa.a: The little ones were nodding, so they probably like that the rules feel familiar and they can join in without long explanations.

grounding: Children design a new terrace game by borrowing rules from kabaddi and tag, giving them a working start.

subtype: Approach: deciding the goal and how someone wins first [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday. "Every game needs a finish line," said Salma, chewing her pencil. Nirmala frowned. "We keep arguing about how to move." "Because we don't know what we're moving for," said Salma. "First: how does someone win?"

Thursday. In the playground the group agreed: each team hides flags in its half, and whichever team gathers five flags first wins.

Saturday. Now the rules came easily. Runners could step only on the chalk squares, and nobody could carry more than one flag. "If we knew the goal on Tuesday," Nirmala laughed, "we'd have saved two days."

qa.q: How many flags does a team need to win?
qa.a: A team needs five flags to win.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling about the arguments on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nirmala was frustrated, since the group kept arguing about moves without a shared goal.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group have used on Tuesday, and why?
qa.a: They could have borrowed rules from a known game and tested them with a short trial, since that gives a starting point. Starting with the goal still helped make later choices simple.

qa.q: How do the runners' rules look to someone who joins late?
qa.a: A newcomer would see clear limits, such as the chalk squares and one flag at a time, and could join without asking the whole story because the goal is simple.

grounding: A girl points out a game needs an end, the group sets the first-to-five-flags goal and builds movement rules around it.

subtype: Approach: playing a quick trial round to test it [Action]
passage: In the schoolyard in Valencia, Diego drew a line in chalk and said, "Let's just try it for five minutes." Nobody stopped to write every rule. Hiroshi and three others ran between two trees, tagging and passing a ball. After the first round, Hiroshi sighed. "Lucía wins every time. She's too fast." Diego looked at the others' faces and saw the same thing. "Then in the final stretch, runners must hop." They tried again. Lucía hopped, laughing, and this time Hiroshi got there first. Nobody minded losing, and they kept playing until the bell.

qa.q: How long did the children try the game at first?
qa.a: They tried the game for five minutes.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi feel after the first round, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hiroshi felt discouraged, shown by the sigh and the complaint that Lucía always wins.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the children use to make it fair, and why?
qa.a: They could give the fastest runner a handicap, such as a later start, or switch roles each round. Both keep the game fun for everyone while staying easy to explain.

qa.q: How does Lucía experience the new hopping rule?
qa.a: Lucía hopped and laughed, so the rule seems to make the game more playful for Lucía too, even though winning is no longer certain.

grounding: Children play a quick trial round without fixing every rule, notice the fast runner always wins and add a hopping rule.
